tldr: Researchers have developed QLAUN, a 15 kg torque-controlled quadruped robot whose main body parts are completely 3D-printed. Its modular, electronics-free leg design makes it easy to build, operate, and repair even for budget-constrained labs.
hero_caption: A comparison between Marc Raibert's early quadruped robot from 1986 and QLAUN, the platform presented in this 2024 work. It highlights the evolution from early, large-scale hydraulic and pneumatic systems to modern, fully 3D-printed, modular electric quadruped robots at a glance.
overview:
Research in quadrupedal robotics demands extensive expertise across mechanical design, locomotion control, state estimation, and path planning, alongside substantial R&D budgets. For universities and small research institutions with limited funding, purchasing expensive commercial robots or repairing damaged components at high costs has been an exceptionally high barrier. While open-source, lightweight platforms such as SOLO exist, there is still a shortage of affordable machines that balance agility with sufficient payload capacity and practical robustness.

To empower robotics research in Lebanon and the broader Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region, the authors developed QLAUN (Quad-Legged Adaptive Unmanned Navigator), an affordable quadruped robot designed to achieve both robustness and agility. By adopting an almost completely 3D-printed design primarily using PLA filament and combining it with off-the-shelf BLDC motors and belt transmissions, the platform enables remarkably low-cost fabrication.

In its hardware design, QLAUN introduces an electronics-free leg strategy that eliminates circuit boards inside the leg modules, allowing each leg to be detached and swapped quickly using just three bolts. For actuation, custom 3D-printed helical planetary gearboxes (8:1) are paired with belt transmissions (4:1) to form a 32:1 Quasi-Direct Drive (QDD) powertrain, striking a balance between high torque output and backdrivability.

This study demonstrates that a 15 kg torque-controlled quadruped robot can be built at a practical level using only off-the-shelf components and 3D printing. The platform is planned to be open-sourced and offered as fully assembled units, providing a wide range of researchers with an accessible foundation for locomotion control and SLAM experiments.
contributions: Achieved dramatically low costs by 3D-printing the primary structure and gearboxes in PLA and pairing them with off-the-shelf, commercial components.
Proposed an electronics-free leg structure with zero electronics housed inside the leg modules, enabling instant replacement and customization using just three bolts.
Constructed a QDD actuation system with an overall 32:1 reduction ratio by combining helical planetary gears (8:1) and timing belts (4:1), achieving both high torque and excellent backdrivability.
Designed a bio-inspired leg mechanism based on canine skeletal proportions (1:1 thigh-to-shank ratio) and compliant TPU feet to mitigate impacts and improve terrain adaptation.

sections.heading: Why is a 3D-printed quadruped robot needed now?
sections.summary: While quadruped robots have evolved from early prismatic legs to articulated legs, research platforms remain prohibitively expensive. To bridge the gap between agility, payload capacity, and low cost, the authors introduce QLAUN.
sections.details:
The history of quadruped robots traces back to Marc Raibert's prismatic leg model in 1986. Prismatic legs featured two degrees of freedom—hip rotation and leg extension—laying the groundwork for early locomotion research. Over time, designs evolved into articulated legs with rotational hip and knee joints, and eventually redundant articulated legs with added ankle joints, unlocking greater flexibility and locomotion performance.

However, building these robots requires multidisciplinary expertise spanning mechanical engineering, control, and perception, along with significant funding. For smaller, underfunded research labs, acquiring such platforms has been financially out of reach. While lightweight open-source platforms like SOLO (around 2.2 kg) are agile and affordable, their payload capacity is inherently limited. On the other hand, heavy platforms such as Kirin—which can carry 125 kg on a 50 kg body—are optimized for load-bearing and lack the agility seen in robots like Spot or ANYmal.

What the community needed was a robust platform that balances high mobility with practical payload capacity, while remaining cheap to repair when damaged. To address this, the authors created QLAUN, an affordable, modular, torque-controlled robot whose primary components can be fabricated on desktop 3D printers.

sections.heading: The hardware powering QLAUN: Thorough engineering from gearboxes to leg modules
sections.summary: Weighing 15 kg with 12 DoF, QLAUN incorporates high-torque QDD actuators using 3D-printed planetary gearboxes and belt drives. The legs feature a fully modular, wiring-free design that can be replaced with just three bolts.
sections.details:
The robot's hardware was designed with modularity and maintainability as top priorities.

### II-A Actuator Design
Each joint is driven by a custom Quasi-Direct Drive (QDD) mechanism. The motor is an off-the-shelf brushless DC motor commonly used in drones (mjbots MJ5208, 330KV, 600W), coupled with a 3D-printed 8:1 planetary gearbox. By adopting helical gears, the design minimizes backlash while improving torque transmission efficiency. Joint positions are tracked using high-resolution incremental encoders (AMT 103-V, 2048 PPR), driven by ODrive Pro controllers capable of Field-Oriented Control (FOC). Operating at a 20V battery voltage and a maximum current of 30A, the actuator can output up to 5 N·m of torque even when capped at a conservative 40% of the motor's rated capacity.

### II-B Leg Design
Dubbed the "RAPID Leg," each leg features 3 degrees of freedom (DoF): Hip Abduction-Adduction (HAA), Hip Flexion-Extension (HFE), and Knee Flexion-Extension (KFE). The leg mechanism includes several key design innovations:
- **Canine-inspired link ratio**: The thigh and shank lengths are set to a 1:1 ratio, mirroring canine anatomy to enhance locomotion efficiency.
- **Torque amplification and decoupling via belt drives**: A 4:1 timing belt transmission is integrated into the HFE and KFE joints. Combined with the actuator's 8:1 reduction, this yields an overall 32:1 gear ratio, delivering ample joint torque.
- **Electronics-free design**: No sensors, boards, or wiring are housed within the leg modules. Consequently, an entire leg assembly can be swapped by removing just three bolts.
- **Compliant foot**: The foot tips are 3D-printed from flexible thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU-95A) to cushion severe impacts during foot-ground collisions.

### II-C System Design
The complete robot measures 38 cm in height, 77 cm in length, and 38 cm in width, with a total weight of approximately 15 kg. Its main chassis is also 3D-printed from PLA, offering broad expandability to mount sensor arrays or robotic manipulator arms.

sections.heading: Future outlook: Open-source release and expanding robotics from the MENA region
sections.summary: QLAUN was demonstrated as a robust, agile, and cost-effective research platform. Moving forward, the team plans to validate SLAM and rough-terrain locomotion control while releasing the design files and software to the global open-source community.
sections.details:
QLAUN was developed to invigorate robotics research across the MENA region, starting from the Lebanese American University (LAU). It demonstrates a viable path to building high-performance, torque-controlled robots using accessible 3D printers and off-the-shelf parts, without relying on costly commercial systems.

Upcoming work will focus on deploying the platform for advanced research tasks, including robust locomotion control algorithms, LiDAR-based SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping), and terrain-adaptation experiments on unknown, uneven surfaces.

Furthermore, the hardware 3D models and control software will be released freely to the global community as an open-source initiative, with pre-assembled units also planned for distribution. This effort aims to allow researchers worldwide—regardless of their budget—to conduct cutting-edge legged locomotion experiments.

takeaways: Keeping legs completely electronics-free (no internal boards or wiring) yields exceptional maintainability and modularity, enabling leg swaps with just a few bolts.

Stacking a 3D-printed helical planetary gearbox (8:1) and a timing belt drive (4:1) on a commercial BLDC motor provides an affordable way to achieve a 32:1 torque multiplication alongside high backdrivability.
Strategically combining rigid PLA for structural frames and compliant TPU for foot pads provides sufficient impact resistance even for a 15 kg quadruped robot.
limitations: As an extended abstract, the paper does not include dynamic experimental benchmarks from physical trials, such as maximum running speed, jumping performance, or continuous battery runtime.
Because the structural frame and reduction gears are printed from PLA, questions remain regarding thermal deformation and gear tooth wear during prolonged, high-load operation.
Because the electronics-free leg design avoids routing wiring into the legs, integrating direct tactile or contact force sensing at the footpads would require mechanical and wiring redesigns.
